strengths: The method exposes a meaningful interpretability vulnerability: matching input gradients near initialization and a chosen target redirects activation maximization through weight fine-tuning, without adding conspicuous architectural components.

Pixel- and Fourier-domain examples convincingly demonstrate targeted visualization changes. Multiple similarity metrics, preservation-weight sweeps, and 16 width/depth configurations provide useful empirical characterization.

The presentation provides an intuitive mechanism, explicit losses, substantial implementation details, and a code link. Computational limitations and unsuccessful defenses are reported candidly. The experiments raise no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving model behavior with minimal performance impact is overstated. The main CIFAR-10 example reduces accuracy from 86.33% to 82.39% and target-class AUROC from 0.970 to 0.938; Figure 5 reports still larger accuracy losses in several settings. Aggregate accuracy and AUROC also do not establish preservation of individual predictions or learned representations.

The auditing claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Experiments manipulate selected output units on MNIST and CIFAR-10 using a few target images, without testing hidden neurons or concealing an actual backdoor or spurious feature. The principal attack evaluation fixes a known initialization distribution and gradient-ascent procedure, leaving effectiveness across broader auditing configurations uncertain.

Although the distinction from architecture-modifying attacks is clear, there are no empirical attack baselines or ablations isolating the contributions of the slingshot and landing zones. Comparisons with simpler fine-tuning objectives would better establish the method's contribution beyond existing gradient-based explanation manipulation.

The defenses remain exploratory: only one attacked model per dataset is evaluated, without adaptive attackers. Removing the target often fails to recover the original concept, and the combined defense performs poorly. Switching to Adam also reduces the learning rate, confounding the optimizer comparison. These findings do not substantiate a reliable protective measure.

The theoretical argument needs qualification. Equation (7) does not ensure differentiability at the target when the landing zone becomes a singleton, so the claimed stationarity does not follow generally. Appendix A also describes a sufficient landing-radius bound as necessary. The idealized construction does not establish convergence for the network obtained through finite-sample gradient matching.

Despite the useful implementation details, the manuscript leaves independent attack-training repetitions, confidence-interval construction, precise stopping criteria, and construction of the nonstandard 80/20 dataset splits unclear. Reported variability across generated visualizations does not establish reliability across independently trained attacks.
